analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil and gas commodity trading profits at regular income rates instead of the lower capital gains rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in August 2009 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required profits from trading oil and natural gas commodities — including futures, derivatives, and index contracts — to be taxed as short-term, ordinary income at regular rates, instead of at the lower capital gains rate that speculators currently receive. It also would have removed the tax exemption for tax-exempt organizations (such as pension funds or endowments) making money on oil and gas trades, subjecting those gains to the unrelated business income tax. The provisions applied to commodities acquired between September 1, 2009 and January 1, 2014, and the bill directed Treasury to study and report on the tax treatment of commodity contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who pay regular income tax rates on their wages while commodity speculators would pay the same rates on oil and gas trading profits, closing a gap that currently favors financial traders. Any federal revenue raised would come from investors in energy commodities rather than from wage earners. Consumers could also benefit indirectly if removing a tax advantage for speculative trading reduced pressure on oil and gas prices.

how_it_helps.text: It would close a gap that lets Wall Street traders in oil and natural gas pay the lower long-term capital gains rate — up to 15% at the time — on profits that ordinary workers pay full income tax rates on.
It would stop tax-exempt entities like pension funds and endowments from using their tax-free status to profit from oil and gas speculation without paying unrelated business tax.
It required the Treasury Department to study and report on how tax policy affects commodity exchanges and the demand for, and price of, oil and natural gas.

analysis.who_pays: Investors and institutions that profit from trading oil and natural gas commodities — hedge funds, traders, and tax-exempt entities speculating in energy markets — who would pay ordinary income tax rates (up to 35% at the time) instead of the lower 15% capital gains rate on those profits.

drawbacks.text: Raising taxes on oil and gas trading could increase the cost of hedging and dealing in energy commodities, and opponents of such measures generally argue some of that cost could be passed through to consumers at the pump or in heating bills.

The bill's rules are technically intricate — covering derivatives, partnership interests, and foreign-corporation look-through rules with special anti-avoidance regulations — adding compliance complexity for funds and tax-exempt investors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been a fairer tax code and potentially less tax-favored speculation in oil and gas; the main drawbacks are the disputed question of whether higher taxes on commodity traders raise energy costs for consumers and the administrative complexity of policing derivatives and pass-through structures. On balance it was a targeted tax increase on a wealthy investor class, but its actual effect on gas prices is uncertain and was itself the subject of the bill's required Treasury study [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2009 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken on the bill in the 111th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never had a Senate or House vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas commodity traders and tax-exempt investors speculating in energy commodities kept their lower capital-gains tax treatment; ordinary taxpayers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; had no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Commodity trading and energy financial interests
against.role: Traders, hedge funds, and energy derivatives industry
against.what_they_did: Tax treatment of commodities trading is a high-stakes issue for these firms, which routinely oppose legislation raising their tax rates; no public record of this bill specifically appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party split to show; it was a Democratic-sponsored bill with no cosponsors of any party and no votes.

industries.industry: Commodity and energy traders (hedge funds, swap dealers, Wall Street speculators in oil and gas)
industries.note: The bill would tax their oil and natural gas trading profits at ordinary income rates instead of the lower capital gains rate, raising their tax bill for positions taken between late 2009 and the end of 2013 [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Tax-exempt institutions investing in energy commodities (pension funds, university endowments)
industries.note: Their gains from oil and gas commodity trading would become taxable as unrelated business income, closing a loophole that let them profit tax-free [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and consumers
industries.note: The bill aimed to curb tax-favored speculation that was blamed for inflating energy prices; producers could face more expensive hedging, while consumers could benefit if speculation-driven price pressure eased — though that effect was unproven and was to be studied [S3].
